glossary.Discharge: Fluid coming from the eye; watery, sticky or purulent.
glossary.Grittiness: A feeling like sand in the eye, typical of viral conjunctivitis.
glossary.Crusting: Dried discharge on the lashes, especially on waking.
glossary.Watering: Excess tears running from the eye.
glossary.Sticky eyelids: Lids glued by discharge, suggesting a bacterial cause.
glossary.Cornea: The clear dome at the front of the eye; involvement causes pain, photophobia and blurred vision.
glossary.Pupils: The black central openings of the irises; normal in conjunctivitis.
glossary.Staph aureus: Staphylococcus aureus, a skin bacterium that causes bacterial conjunctivitis.
glossary.Strep: Streptococcus, a bacterium that can cause bacterial conjunctivitis.
glossary.Haemophilus: Haemophilus influenzae, a common bacterial cause of conjunctivitis, especially in children.
glossary.Gonococcus: Neisseria gonorrhoeae; in newborns it causes severe purulent conjunctivitis.
glossary.Hay fever: Seasonal allergic rhinitis caused by pollen.
glossary.Eczema: Itchy inflamed skin condition linked to atopy; can affect the eyelids.
glossary.Rhinitis: Inflammation of the nose lining, causing sneezing and a runny nose.
glossary.Asthma: Chronic airway inflammation with wheeze; part of the atopic picture.
glossary.Seasonal variation: Symptoms that come and go with the time of year, as with pollen allergy.
glossary.Bilateral: Affecting both sides, here both eyes.
glossary.Lid hygiene: Gently cleaning the eyelids and lashes with clean water and cotton wool.
glossary.Cold compress: A cool, damp cloth held on the eye to ease swelling and discomfort.
glossary.Lubricating drops: Eye drops that moisten and soothe the eye surface.
glossary.Artificial tears: Lubricating eye drops that wash out allergens and soothe the eye.
glossary.Hypoallergenic: Unlikely to trigger an allergic reaction.
glossary.Topical: Applied directly to the eye as drops or ointment.
glossary.Ointment: A greasy preparation that stays on the eye longer than drops.
glossary.H1 receptor antagonist: An antihistamine that blocks histamine's H1 receptor, easing itch and redness.
glossary.Sodium cromoglycate: A mast cell stabiliser eye drop for recurrent allergic conjunctivitis; works best used regularly.
glossary.Third trimester: The last three months of pregnancy, from week 28.
glossary.Protein synthesis: The process by which cells build proteins; chloramphenicol blocks it in bacteria.
glossary.Broad-spectrum: Active against many different types of bacteria.
glossary.Systemic absorption: Drug getting into the bloodstream and spreading through the body.
glossary.Neutrophilic: Made up mostly of neutrophils, the white cells that form pus.
glossary.Exudate: Fluid rich in protein and cells leaking from inflamed tissue.
glossary.Reactive: Enlarged in response to nearby infection rather than from disease within the node.
glossary.Neonatal: In the first four weeks after birth.
glossary.Swab: A sample of discharge taken on a cotton-tipped stick for lab testing.
glossary.Contact lenses: Lenses worn on the eye; they raise the risk of keratitis and must be left out during infection.
glossary.Self-care: Treatment the patient manages at home without medicines from a doctor.
glossary.Medial-to-lateral: From the inner corner of the eye towards the outer corner.
glossary.Inflammation: The body's response to injury or infection: redness, swelling, heat and pain.
glossary.Resistance: Bacteria no longer killed or stopped by an antibiotic.
glossary.Eyelid cleansers: Gentle wipes or solutions to clean allergens and debris from the lids.
